A
Analysis A follows the pre‑specified plan of a single test on the full sample, whereas Analysis B repeatedly peeks at the data and stops early without adjusting for multiple looks, inflating the Type I error rate.

B
Analysis A repeatedly checks the data and stops when a p‑value falls below 0.05 without adjusting for multiple looks, which inflates the Type I error rate; Analysis B uses a pre‑specified fixed‑sample test, preserving the nominal significance level.

A
Analysis A conducts a single, pre‑planned test on the full sample, preserving the nominal Type I error rate, whereas Analysis B repeatedly checks the data and stops early upon significance without adjusting for multiple looks, which inflates the false‑positive risk.

B  
Analysis A performs repeated significance checks without adjusting for multiple looks, inflating the Type I error rate, whereas Analysis B uses a pre‑specified fixed‑sample test, which preserves the nominal error rate.

A
Because Analysis A conducts a single pre‑specified test on the full sample, whereas Analysis B repeatedly checks the data and stops early without adjusting for multiple looks, inflating the false‑positive rate.

B  
Analysis B avoids the inflated Type I error from repeated peeking by using a pre‑specified fixed‑sample test, whereas Analysis A’s early‑stopping rule without correction leads to an invalid significance claim.

A  
Analysis A follows the pre‑specified plan and tests the hypothesis only once on the full data, avoiding the inflation of Type I error caused by optional stopping in Analysis B.

B
Analysis A peeks at the data repeatedly and stops early without adjusting for multiple looks, inflating the Type I error rate, whereas Analysis B follows a pre‑specified plan and tests the full sample only once, providing a valid inference.

A  
Analysis A uses only pre‑treatment attributes (customer characteristics and the assigned email arm) to predict conversion, whereas Analysis B incorrectly includes the post‑treatment variable “visit,” which leaks information that would not be available before deciding whom to email and inflates the model’s apparent performance.

B
Analysis B is methodologically sounder because it uses only pre‑treatment predictors, avoiding data leakage from the post‑email visit variable that inflates performance in Analysis A.

A
Analysis B incorrectly includes the post‑treatment conversion variable, which leaks future information and inflates performance, whereas Analysis A uses only pre‑email attributes.

B
Because Analysis A incorrectly includes the post‑email conversion flag as a predictor, causing data leakage and an overly optimistic estimate, whereas Analysis B uses only pre‑treatment information available before the campaign.

A
Because Analysis B incorrectly includes the post‑treatment variable spend as a predictor, causing data leakage and inflating performance, whereas Analysis A uses only pre‑campaign features that would be available when sizing the next month's campaign.

B
Analysis A incorrectly includes the post‑treatment variable spend as a predictor, causing data leakage and an inflated AUC, while Analysis B uses only pre‑treatment features appropriate for forecasting conversion before the email is sent.

A
Analysis A uses only pre‑campaign features, whereas Analysis B incorrectly includes post‑treatment variables (conversion, visit) that would not be available before sending the email, leading to data leakage and an inflated R².

B
Analysis A incorrectly uses post‑treatment outcomes (conversion and visit) as predictors, causing data leakage and an inflated R², whereas Analysis B relies only on pre‑campaign features, providing a valid assessment of forecastability.

A  
Analysis A adjusts for the confounding variable severity by stratifying patients into severity bands and comparing medication effects within each band, whereas Analysis B ignores this confounding and therefore yields a biased estimate.

B
Analysis B adjusts for the confounding variable severity by stratifying patients into severity bands and shows that within each band the medication is associated with faster recovery, whereas Analysis A ignores this important confounder and draws a misleading conclusion.

A  
Analysis A correctly controls for severity, a key confounder that affects both medication assignment and recovery time, yielding an unbiased estimate of the medication’s effect.

B  
Analysis B includes the severity variable, which is a confounder affecting both medication assignment and recovery time, thereby reducing omitted‑variable bias and giving a more credible estimate of the medication’s effect.

A
Analysis A attempts to control for the confounding variable severity by stratifying the Mantel‑Haenszel test, whereas Analysis B ignores confounders and yields a misleading association.

B
Because Analysis B controls for the confounding variable severity by stratifying and using a Mantel‑Haenszel estimate, providing a less biased assessment of the medication’s effect on fast recovery, whereas Analysis A ignores important covariates and yields a misleading result.

A
Because it controls for the hospital confounder by stratifying within each hospital, showing the true direction of the treatment effect, whereas Analysis B pools across hospitals and ignores this important source of bias.

B  
Analysis B accounts for the confounding effect of hospital (and implicitly severity) by estimating treatment effects within each hospital, revealing that the apparent harmful effect in the pooled analysis is due to differing case‑mix across hospitals.

A  
Fisher’s exact test is appropriate for small sample sizes and low expected counts, whereas the two‑proportion z‑test relies on a normal approximation that is invalid when expected cell frequencies are below 5.

B
Fisher's exact test is the appropriate exact test for small sample binary data, whereas the z‑test’s normal approximation is invalid when expected counts are low.

A
Analysis A correctly uses a one‑way ANOVA to compare mean spend across the three categorical channel groups, whereas Analysis B inappropriately treats the nominal channel variable as numeric and computes a Pearson correlation, which assumes an ordered, interval‑scale relationship that does not exist.

B
Analysis B uses a one‑way ANOVA, which appropriately tests for differences in mean spend across the categorical channel groups, whereas Analysis A incorrectly treats the nominal channel variable as numeric and computes a Pearson correlation.

A
The chi‑square test correctly assesses association between a categorical predictor (zip code type) and a binary outcome, whereas treating zip codes as numeric scores and computing a Pearson correlation imposes an unjustified interval scale and linear assumption.

B
Because the chi‑square test correctly evaluates the association between two categorical variables (zip code type and binary conversion), whereas Analysis A inappropriately treats the nominal zip code categories as numeric and uses Pearson correlation, which assumes a linear relationship and continuous data.

A
Analysis A correctly uses a chi‑square test of independence for a categorical predictor (channel) and a binary outcome, whereas Analysis B inappropriately treats the nominal channel variable as numeric and computes a Pearson correlation, which assumes equal intervals and a linear relationship that do not hold here.

B
Because Analysis B correctly uses a chi‑square test for independence between the categorical channel variable and binary conversion, whereas Analysis A incorrectly treats the nominal channel variable as numeric and computes a Pearson correlation.

A
Analysis A properly controls for the multiple subgroup tests using a Holm correction, whereas Analysis B ignores the multiple‑testing problem and overstates significance.

B  
Analysis B applies a multiple‑testing correction (Holm) to control the familywise error rate across the seven segment‑wise tests, whereas Analysis A reports raw p‑values without adjustment, increasing the risk of false‑positive findings.

A
Analysis A properly accounts for the multiple comparisons across history segments by applying a Holm correction, whereas Analysis B ignores this issue and risks inflating Type I error.

B  
Analysis B applies a Holm multiple‑testing correction to control the family‑wise error rate across the seven segment‑wise tests, whereas Analysis A reports raw p‑values without adjustment, increasing the risk of false‑positive findings.

A
Analysis A properly controls for multiple comparisons using a Holm correction, whereas Analysis B reports raw p‑values without adjustment, inflating the risk of false‑positive findings.

B
Analysis B appropriately adjusts for multiple comparisons using the Holm procedure, reducing the risk of false‑positive findings, whereas Analysis A reports raw p‑values without correction.

A
Analysis A properly controls for the inflated Type I error due to testing multiple zip‑code × channel cells by applying a Holm correction, whereas Analysis B ignores this multiplicity and risks reporting spurious significant effects.

B  
Analysis B controls the family‑wise error rate across the nine cell‑wise tests using a Holm correction, reducing the risk of false‑positive findings that Analysis A overlooks.
